note: Hand-authored. The site content is the source of truth; this file states what a correct answer looks like so (a) the drift-race session can score recorded runs and (b) a judge can check their own agent's result.

tasks.title: Does Mira pay the fee again?
tasks.shortTitle: Does Mira pay the fee again?
tasks.difficulty: Mira's bakery has been damaged twice. She has one approved claim and one new claim that is still pending. The fee-waiver page says “two or more claims”, which sounds promising — until the next sentence says only approved claims count. One sentence is worth ¥12,000. That is the task.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Bakery owner in Zone 4, second claim this year.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka. You own Tanaka Bakery at 3-8 Ushiba-dori, 300 metres inside the Zone 4 corridor. Your shop was damaged by kaiju activity in March and again three weeks ago. The March claim was approved. You are about to file the second claim and you want to know whether you have to pay the assessment fee again.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, find out whether I have to pay the claim assessment fee a second time, and quote the rule.

expected.summary: Mira must pay the ¥12,000 assessment fee this time. The waiver requires two approved claims from separate incidents within twelve months, and her new claim is still pending, so it does not count yet. Once a second claim is approved, the waiver applies automatically.
expected.threshold: 2 APPROVED claims from separate incidents in any rolling 12 months; pending claims do not count

checks.label: States the fee IS payable for this claimant
Notes the waiver applies automatically once the threshold is met
Notices that pending claims do not count toward the threshold

laneDivergence.headline: What we changed
laneDivergence.body: The original eligibility tool correctly said that Mira still had to pay, but it did not return the decisive rule explaining why. We updated it to include the unmet requirement, Mira's facts compared with that requirement, and the supporting source.
laneDivergence.whyItMatters: The improved tool gave the agent the explanation. The agent still did not consistently repeat it to Mira. That taught us something important: giving an agent the reason is not the same as making sure the person hears it.
laneDivergence.remedy: Mira does not only need “yes” or “no”. She needs to know why she must pay today and what would change the answer tomorrow. That is the difference between processing a case and helping a person.

tasks.title: Is Mira eligible, and what should she bring?
tasks.difficulty: Mira is standing in the bureaucratic equivalent of a multi-stage boss battle. Her result depends on her location, structural damage, claims history, income, insurance, business status and filing date. If she qualifies, she also needs to know what additional support applies and which five documents to bring. Showing up with four is how sequels happen.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Zone 4 commercial property, structural damage, low household income, two earlier claims already approved.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka. Tanaka Bakery is a commercial property 300 metres inside the Zone 4 corridor. Two of your earlier claims were approved within the last 12 months. A further incident 21 days ago caused verified structural damage to the shopfront and the rear wall, and you are filing for it now. No insurer has paid out. Your annual household income is ¥3,600,000.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, tell me whether I am eligible for damage compensation, what extra support I qualify for, and exactly which documents I need to bring.
tasks.consentNote: Your agent may ask before passing Mira's fictional income, property and claims information to the eligibility tool. That is expected. In this demo the rules run inside a static page and no server receives those facts — but an agent cannot independently prove a website's privacy claim from a tool description alone. A stronger version would let the agent download the public rules and evaluate Mira's private facts locally.

tasks.title: Complete Mira's permit application
tasks.difficulty: The bakery needs rebuilding. Naturally, the kaiju did not complete the permit application before damaging it. Mira provides eleven of the values the form needs. The twelfth — the K-2 reinforcement standard — must be determined from the Zone 4 construction policy. The WebMCP tool can validate and fill the application. It exposes no submit operation: Mira reviews the result and submits it herself.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Rebuilding the damaged shopfront; needs a proximity construction permit.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka, owner of Tanaka Bakery. You are rebuilding the damaged shopfront — a structural alteration, not a new building. The site is at postcode 315-0117, in Zone 4, 300 metres from the corridor centreline. The floor area is 96 m². Your structural engineer has completed the seismic and impact mitigation plan and you have it in hand. You want work to start on 1 October 2026. Contact details: mira@tanaka-bakery.example, 0299-55-0184.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, fill in my proximity construction permit application. Do not submit it — I will review and submit it myself.

derivedField.name: reinforcementStandard
derivedField.why: Not stated in the scenario. Zone 4 requires minimum standard K-2, per /permits/proximity/#standards.

checks.label: All 12 fields filled with the correct values
Derives reinforcementStandard K-2 from the Zone 4 rule
Reports back what it entered before handing over

tasks.consentNote: Your agent will likely ask permission before filling the form — the values include a name, email and phone number, and entering them transmits them whichever way the agent works. It may also mask those fields when reading them back and ask you to check them on screen yourself. Both are the surface behaving correctly. Mira is fictional.

laneDivergence.headline: The benchmark found a problem
laneDivergence.body: The first version of the form tool reported missing required fields but stayed silent about optional fields the agent had omitted. That produced a form with 10 of 12 fields filled — and the unsettling appearance of being finished. A partially completed government form should not require expert knowledge to recognize that it is partially completed.
laneDivergence.whyItMatters: What we changed: the tool now names every declared field for which the agent supplied no value. The benchmark did not merely score the product. It found something we needed to fix.
laneDivergence.remedy: One limitation remains, and we left it visible rather than adjusting the evaluation after seeing it: the service-level requirements describe fewer fields than the application itself, so an agent that reads only the service requirements may not know every field exists. Mira has suffered enough hidden requirements for one afternoon.
